transcript.text: This is the Paper Library daily on Polygenic risk prediction, for Tuesday, November 24.
Let's turn to polygenic risk prediction, where both new preprints are about tradeoffs you can't see when a pipeline hands you one best model.

The first is from the Xu lab, posted on Research Square. Cross-ancestry scores predict unevenly across populations, so the authors built a shrinkage framework called cluster fixed. It uses known ancestry labels to map the whole Pareto frontier between overall accuracy and fairness across groups.

They simulated phenotypes on 1000 Genomes genotypes. When effects were mostly shared across groups, worst-case subgroup disparity fell by 71.7 percent, but global accuracy dropped by 57.8 percent. When population-specific effects were large, fairness and accuracy could both improve.

With Pan-UK Biobank height effect estimates, disparity fell by 50.5 to 70.3 percent on chromosomes 1 and 21, and other correction strategies didn't match those gains. But that's one trait and two chromosomes, and the authors say it still needs testing in other traits and cohorts.

The second is from the Tucker-Drob lab, on medRxiv. GWAS estimation error biases score accuracy downward, so the authors used GWAS run in independent samples to correct for it. They then asked how much SNP heritability clumping, LDpred2, SBayesR and PRS-CS-auto really capture.

They also give a way to split existing summary statistics into independent halves synthetically. The finding is that methods that shrink effects hard look better on raw accuracy but worse after correction. LDpred2-inf has lower raw accuracy, but after correction it nearly recovers the full SNP heritability.
They also report that aggressive shrinkage can bias associations with other phenotypes, even after error correction. That matters for anyone using scores as covariates in downstream analyses.
So both papers say the same thing: the single number we usually optimize, whether raw accuracy or pooled performance, can hide a tradeoff you should choose on purpose.

papers.title: Fixed group shrinkage exposes the fairness accuracy Pareto frontier for cross ancestry polygenic risk scores
Quantification of Bias-Variance Tradeoffs in Genome-Wide Polygenic Indices: When 'Good' PGIs are Bad and 'Bad' PGIs are Good
